Covariance matrix of the graph-layer parameters

Source: R/methods.R
mc_vcov_graph.Rd

Returns the estimated covariance matrix of the graph-layer parameter vector \(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}\) of a fitted mcglm_graph object in the three forms the package supports: model-based, empirical sandwich, and sandwich corrected for the estimation of the first stage.

Usage

mc_vcov_graph(
  fit,
  type = c("model", "sandwich", "two_stage"),
  cluster = NULL,
  small_sample = FALSE,
  method = c("auto", "shortcut", "full"),
  sensitivity = c("observed", "expected")
)

Arguments

fit

an object of class "mcglm_graph".

type

"model" for \(\mathbf J_n^{-1}\), "sandwich" for the empirical sandwich, or "two_stage" for the sandwich corrected for the estimation of the residuals.

cluster

optional vector with one identifier per observational row. With type = "sandwich" or "two_stage", the contributions are summed within clusters before the variability is formed, which is the form to use when the unit of dependence is not the row of the data matrix. It must have no missing value and at least two distinct values; the default NULL takes the rows as the units. It is refused with type = "model".

small_sample

logical, default FALSE; multiply the clustered variability by \(G/(G-1)\), with \(G\) the number of clusters. It has no effect without cluster and is refused with type = "model".

method

for type = "two_stage", the route of the correction: "shortcut", "full", or "auto" (default). "auto" takes the full form when it is available and either a response has a variance function other than "constant" or the fitted DAG has an immorality; in every other case it takes the shortcut when it applies and the full form when it does not. The full form rebuilds the first stage and is slower. It has no meaning for the other two types.

sensitivity

for the full form, "observed" (default) or "expected", the sensitivity of the first stage described in the section "The full form".

Value

A \(q_{\mathcal G} \times q_{\mathcal G}\) symmetric matrix, with \(q_{\mathcal G}\) the number of graph parameters and their names in its dimnames, carrying the attributes "type", "variability", "edge_pos" (positions of the edge parameters), "n_clusters", "small_sample", which is TRUE exactly when the factor \(G/(G-1)\) was applied, and the inversion diagnostics "inversion_status" and "inversion_ridge" of the sensitivity solve (with type = "model" also "inversion_rcond", the reciprocal condition number met by that solve). "n_clusters" is NA without cluster. With type = "two_stage" it also carries "two_stage_method", the route taken, and either the factor "Q" the shortcut applies, \([\mathbf K_b\dot{\boldsymbol \Sigma}_{b,d}]_{rr}/(2m_r)\), with the averages \(m_r\) in "center", or, for the full form, the cross sensitivity "B", the first-stage sensitivity "A", both on the accumulated scale, which "sensitivity" was used and its reciprocal condition number "sensitivity_rcond". The function refuses fits whose numerical diagnostics mark graph-layer inference as uncertified.

Details

The graph parameters solve second-order (Pearson) estimating functions \(\mathbf U_n(\boldsymbol\theta)=\sum_i\boldsymbol\psi_i(\boldsymbol\theta)\) built on the Pearson residuals of the first-stage MCGLM (Bonat and Jorgensen, 2016). Write \(\mathbf J=-E(\partial\boldsymbol\psi_i/\partial \boldsymbol\theta^\top)\) for the sensitivity and \(\mathbf V=\lim_n n^{-1}\sum_i\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol\psi_i)\) for the variability, both per unit. The Godambe information is \(\mathbf G=\mathbf J^\top\mathbf V^{-1}\mathbf J\). With the number of responses fixed and the number of units \(n\to\infty\), under regularity conditions that include estimating functions unbiased at \(\boldsymbol\theta_0\) for every unit or cluster, with independent contributions over units or clusters, a root \(\boldsymbol\theta_0\) that is interior and locally unique, a nonsingular \(\mathbf J\), a finite and positive definite \(\mathbf V\) with a Lindeberg condition, and uniform control of the fourth moments of the residuals, $$\sqrt n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}-\boldsymbol\theta_0)\xrightarrow{d} \mathcal N\left(\mathbf 0,\;\mathbf G^{-1}\right),\qquad \mathbf G^{-1}=\mathbf J^{-1}\mathbf V\mathbf J^{-\top}$$ (Godambe, 1960; Jorgensen and Knudsen, 2004). The matrix returned estimates \(n^{-1}\mathbf G^{-1}\), the covariance of \(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}\) itself. With independent clusters the same statement holds for the cluster sums of the contributions, with the number of clusters in the place of \(n\). The robustness of the sandwich is to the fourth-order structure around the root identified by the estimating functions; it does not correct bias from a misspecified mean or second-order covariance, and it treats the graph as fixed.

With type = "model" the covariance is the model-based \(\mathbf J_n^{-1}\), valid under the working identity \(\mathbf V = \mathbf J\) when the relevant second moment is correctly specified and Gaussian fourth-moment identities hold. With type = "sandwich", also called the naive sandwich because it takes the Pearson residuals as observed, it is \(\mathbf H_n^{-1}\mathbf V_n\mathbf H_n^{-1}\), with \(\mathbf H_n\) the curvature of the section "Scale convention" and \(\mathbf V_n=n\widehat{\mathbf V}\) the sum of the outer products of the Pearson contributions, an empirical fourth-moment variability that does not assume that identity. In the DAG layer its block for the structural coefficients of a node is the heteroskedasticity-consistent estimator of White (1980) for the least-squares regression of the centered residual of that node on those of its parents. The unit contribution to the estimating function of parameter \(\theta_d\) is $$\psi_{d,i}=-\tfrac12\left\{\operatorname{tr}(\boldsymbol\Sigma_b^{-1} \dot{\boldsymbol\Sigma}_{b,d})-\mathbf r_i^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_b^{-1} \dot{\boldsymbol\Sigma}_{b,d}\boldsymbol\Sigma_b^{-1}\mathbf r_i\right\},$$ and \(\widehat{\mathbf V}=n^{-1}\sum_i\boldsymbol\psi_i\boldsymbol\psi_i^\top\), where \(\mathbf r_i\) is the vector of centered Pearson residuals of unit \(i\). This empirical variability requires scores centered in expectation for each independent unit or cluster, or a vanishing aggregate of their squared means. A zero total score at the fitted root does not establish that condition under heterogeneous second-moment misspecification. With cluster, the scores are summed by cluster before taking outer products; independence of those clusters remains an assumption about the data.

Scale convention

The model-based sensitivity stored in fit$graph$J is on the accumulated scale, \(\mathbf J_n=n\mathbf J\), while the variability above is per unit. For a sparse DAG, the empirical sandwich and two-stage correction use the observed negative Hessian \(\mathbf H_n\) of the working criterion. Its parent blocks use the residual sample covariance; it can differ from \(\mathbf J_n\) if the DAG misses second-moment structure. For the linear-precision GGM they coincide. The empirical matrix returned here is \(\mathbf H_n^{-1}(n\widehat{\mathbf V})\mathbf H_n^{-1}\), which is the covariance of \(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}\) and not of \(\sqrt n\,\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}\), so its square roots are directly comparable with the estimates returned by coef(fit, type = "graph").

Propagating the first stage

The first two forms refer to the second stage conditionally on the estimated Pearson residuals: they carry the sampling variability of the estimating functions of the graph layer and not the uncertainty inherited from the first-stage fit. type = "two_stage" propagates it, with the number of responses fixed, \(n\to\infty\) and the regularity conditions of the Details holding for the stacked system. Stacking the two sets of estimating functions gives a block triangular sensitivity, and block inversion gives the influence function of the second stage, $$\mathrm{IF}_i=\mathbf H^{-1}\left(\boldsymbol\psi_i-\mathbf B \mathbf A^{-1}\boldsymbol\psi_{\alpha,i}\right),\qquad \mathbf B=-E\!\left(\frac{\partial\boldsymbol\psi_i} {\partial\boldsymbol\alpha^\top}\right).$$ Here \(\mathbf H=-E(\partial\boldsymbol\psi_i/\partial \boldsymbol\theta^\top)\) is the curvature of the graph block under the distribution of the data, estimated by the observed curvature \(\mathbf H_n/n\), and \(\mathbf A=-E(\partial \boldsymbol\psi_{\alpha,i}/\partial\boldsymbol\alpha^\top)\) is the sensitivity of the first stage, whose parameters are \(\boldsymbol\alpha\); both are taken nonsingular. The covariance of \(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}\) is \(n^{-1}\mathbf H^{-1}\widetilde{\mathbf V}\mathbf H^{-\top}\) with $$\widetilde{\mathbf V}=\mathbf V_{\theta\theta} -\mathbf B\mathbf A^{-1}\mathbf V_{\alpha\theta} -\mathbf V_{\theta\alpha}\mathbf A^{-\top}\mathbf B^\top +\mathbf B\mathbf A^{-1}\mathbf V_{\alpha\alpha}\mathbf A^{-\top} \mathbf B^\top,$$ where \(\mathbf V_{\alpha\alpha}\), \(\mathbf V_{\alpha\theta}\) and \(\mathbf V_{\theta\theta}\) are the blocks of the variability of the stacked contributions. The first two types keep only \(\mathbf V_{\theta\theta}\); the difference between the corrected and the naive covariance has no determined sign. This is the correction of Murphy and Topel (1985) and, as a stacked system, the two-step result of Newey and McFadden (1994, Theorem 6.1).

When every response carries a single dispersion parameter that multiplies its variance function (a Poisson-Tweedie variance only with its power fixed at one), the within-response structure is the identity and the prior weights are constant, the first-stage term can be written, to first order, with second-stage quantities only. This is the reduced form, and these three conditions are those of the shortcut below. It also uses that the first stage estimates the correlation between responses without restriction, as mcglm does, and that the first stage acts on the residual covariance as a diagonal rescaling, for which conditions (a) to (c) of the section "What the correction reaches" are sufficient: $$\mathbf B\mathbf A^{-1}\boldsymbol\psi_{\alpha,i}=\mathbf Q (\mathbf r_i\circ\mathbf r_i-\mathbf m),\qquad Q_{dr}=\frac{1}{2m_r}\bigl[\mathbf K_b\dot{\boldsymbol\Sigma}_{b,d} \mathbf K_b\widehat{\mathbf S}_e\bigr]_{rr},\qquad \dot{\boldsymbol\Sigma}_{b,d}=\partial\boldsymbol\Sigma_b/\partial\theta_d,$$ with \(\circ\) the elementwise product, \(\mathbf K_b= \boldsymbol\Sigma_b^{-1}\), \(\widehat{\mathbf S}_e\) the sample covariance of the Pearson residuals and \(m_r\) the average of the squared centered Pearson residuals of response \(r\), which, with constant prior weights and residuals that average zero, is the value at which the first-stage Pearson equations fix it. Since \(r_{ri}^2\) scales as \(1/\tau_r\), unit \(i\) moves \(\log\hat\tau_r\) by \((r_{ri}^2-m_r)/(n m_r)\), which is where the factor \(1/m_r\) comes from. Without the bias correction of mcglm (control_algorithm = list(correct = FALSE)) \(m_r=1\). With it, its default, and unit weights, \(m_r=(n-p_r)/n\) when the responses share the design (or there is a single response), \(p_r\) the number of regression parameters: exactly for the constant variance function with the identity link and for power two with the log link, and closely for the other multiplicative variance functions. A constant weight \(w_0\) turns \(p_r/n\) into \(p_r/(nw_0^2)\), and with designs that differ \(m_r\) is the observed average, slightly below one. Centering on \(m_r\) makes the correction term sum to zero in the sample, and a parameter the first stage fixes exactly, such as the innovation variance of a root node of a DAG with Gaussian intercept-only margins, gets a zero standard error. The shortcut, which is what method = "shortcut" computes, is the reduced form evaluated at the fitted covariance, \(Q_{dr}=[\mathbf K_b\dot{\boldsymbol\Sigma}_{b,d}]_{rr}/(2m_r)\). The two coincide in every row of \(\mathbf Q\) whose entries the fitted and the sample covariances agree on: at every support of the GGM layer, and for the parameters of every node of a DAG without immoralities. For the parameters of a collider with non-adjacent parents, and of its descendants, the shortcut is a first-order approximation, across every response column of the parent block, the parents included, that also needs the DAG to be correctly specified; for the parameters of every other node it equals the reduced form. The full form evaluates \(\mathbf B\) at the data from the first-stage contributions and needs none of these conditions.

When the shortcut is right

The statements of this section are of first order, with the number of responses fixed, \(n\to\infty\) and expectations read as limits of averages over independent units. The reduced form rests on two facts of different kinds. One is algebraic: under the three conditions of the previous section, and with the correlation between responses of the first stage unrestricted, the squared Pearson residual of each response, minus its average over the units, is a linear combination of the centered first-stage contributions of the same unit, whatever the data. That is what mc_two_stage_available checks. The other is statistical. Let \(\mathbf M(\boldsymbol\alpha)=E\{\mathbf r_i(\boldsymbol\alpha) \mathbf r_i(\boldsymbol\alpha)^\top\}\) be the second moment of the Pearson residuals as a function of the first-stage parameters and \(\mathbf M_0\) its value at their limit, which has unit diagonal. Let the Pearson residuals have mean zero at that limit, so that centering them, as the graph layer does, changes neither \(\mathbf M_0\) nor its derivatives. The reduced form holds when every first-stage parameter \(\alpha_m\) moves \(\mathbf M\) as a diagonal rescaling, that is, when for some diagonal matrix \(\boldsymbol\Lambda_m\) $$\frac{\partial\mathbf M}{\partial\alpha_m}= -(\boldsymbol\Lambda_m\mathbf M_0+\mathbf M_0\boldsymbol\Lambda_m)$$ on the diagonal and in the entries that the matrices \(\mathbf K_b \dot{\boldsymbol\Sigma}_{b,d}\mathbf K_b\) read: the edges in the GGM layer, the block of each node and its parents in the DAG layer. Conditions (b) and (c) of the section "What the correction reaches", the latter with \(\mathbf M_0\) in the place of \(\boldsymbol\Sigma_b\), give it, with \(\boldsymbol\Lambda_m=\operatorname{Diag}\{E(\partial\log\varsigma_{ri}/ \partial\alpha_m)\}\). They are sufficient and can be weakened in two ways:

  • (c) can be replaced by \(E(\mathbf r_i\mathbf r_i^\top\mid \mathbf x_i)=c(\mathbf x_i)\mathbf M_0\), with \(c\) a positive function common to the responses, and \(\boldsymbol\Lambda_m\) then carries \(E\{c(\mathbf x_i)\,\partial\log\varsigma_{ri}/\partial\alpha_m\}\). When every response has the constant variance function (c) is not needed in any form, whatever the link, because \(\partial\log\varsigma_{ri}/\partial\alpha_m\) is then the same for every unit;

  • (b) is used only to give the Pearson residuals mean zero and to make \(E(r_{si}\,\varsigma_{ri}^{-1}\partial\mu_{ri}/\partial \boldsymbol\beta_r)=\mathbf 0\) for every pair of responses \((r,s)\). When all responses have the same design, with an intercept, and the variance function and the link make that vector the row of the design times a factor that is the same for every unit, as the constant variance function with the identity link and the Tweedie variance function of power fixed at two with the log link do, the quasi-score equations of the first stage make the Pearson residuals orthogonal to the design in the sample, and (b) is not needed. In the first of these two cases the reduced form then holds with no condition on the mean or on the conditional second moments. In the second, (c), or its weaker form, is required of the Pearson residuals about the limit of the fitted mean; when it holds for those about the true mean, a misspecified mean violates it only at second order in the relative difference between the two means.

Outside these cases the shortcut can omit a term of first order, whose sign is not determined. That is so for a mean that misses a covariate when the designs of the responses differ and, with a variance function that depends on the mean, for a residual correlation that moves with the covariates; the variances of the partial correlations can then be affected as well. The full form needs none of these conditions: with the observed sensitivity it estimates the influence function of Newey and McFadden (1994, Theorem 6.1) whenever the contributions of each unit, row or cluster, to the estimating functions of both stages have zero mean at their limits and the units are independent. Where both routes apply and the conditions hold they agree to first order; where the conditions fail, the full form is the one to use, and method = "full" asks for it. A bootstrap that resamples independent units or clusters and refits both stages (mc_graph_bootstrap) propagates the first stage by construction and is the reference against which both routes can be checked.

The full form

Outside the shortcut the three pieces are formed from the first stage itself. The fitted MCGLM is rebuilt at its estimate with the routines of mcglm, and split into contributions \(\boldsymbol\psi_{\alpha,u}\) of its quasi-score and Pearson functions over units \(u\); \(\mathbf A\) is its sensitivity; and \(\mathbf B\) is formed by the chain rule on the Pearson residual \(r_{ri}=(y_{ri}-\mu_{ri})/\varsigma_{ri}\), \(\varsigma_{ri}^2=C_{(ri),(ri)}\), $$-\frac{\partial r_{ri}}{\partial\boldsymbol\alpha}= \frac{1}{\varsigma_{ri}}\frac{\partial\mu_{ri}}{\partial\boldsymbol\alpha} +r_{ri}\frac{\partial\log\varsigma_{ri}}{\partial\boldsymbol\alpha},$$ with no condition on the mean or on the residual covariance. The correlations between responses of the first stage do not enter \(\varsigma_{ri}\), so their block of \(\mathbf B\) is zero.

The sensitivity \(\mathbf A\) of the first stage is where the full form departs from what mcglm reports. By default, sensitivity = "observed", it is the Jacobian at the estimate of the first-stage estimating equations as mcglm solved them, its bias correction of the Pearson equations included when the fit used it (fit$con$correct), formed by central differences of their totals, each one rebuilt with the routines of mcglm. Divided by the number of units it estimates the matrix the influence function asks for whether or not the mean and the variance function of the first stage are correctly specified. With sensitivity = "expected" \(\mathbf A\) takes its model-based form, with blocks \(\mathbf D^\top\mathbf C^{-1}\mathbf W\mathbf D\) for the regression parameters, \(\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf C^{-1}\dot{\mathbf C}_\lambda\mathbf W \mathbf C^{-1}\dot{\mathbf C}_{\lambda'})\) for the covariance parameters \(\lambda\) and the same trace with \(\partial\mathbf C/\partial \beta\) in the place of \(\dot{\mathbf C}_{\lambda'}\) for the covariance parameters on the regression parameters, where \(\mathbf D\) is the derivative of the stacked means, \(\mathbf C\) the first-stage covariance and \(\mathbf W\) the diagonal matrix of prior weights. It is cheaper and estimates the same limit when the mean and the covariance of the first stage are correctly specified; the corrected covariances of the two forms then differ by a term of order at most \(n^{-1/2}\) relative to the naive sandwich. For a parameter whose corrected variance vanishes to first order, as that of the innovation variance of a root node of a DAG does when the first stage fixes the average of the squared residuals of that response and their mean is zero at the limit, the variance reported under either form is of lower order than the naive one, and the two forms can differ by as much as their own size. When the mean or the variance function of the first stage is misspecified the expected form in general no longer estimates \(\mathbf A\), the difference between the two corrected covariances can be of first order, and the observed sensitivity is the one to use. The observed form inherits the conditioning of the first stage: when that stage is weakly identified, as a Poisson-Tweedie fit whose estimated power and dispersion trade off against each other can be, its Jacobian is close to singular and the propagated variance is numerically unstable. The attribute "sensitivity_rcond" reports the reciprocal condition number of the sensitivity used, and comparing the two forms on the same fit is a direct check. Either way the block of the covariance parameters on the regression parameters is kept: the joint_inv_sensitivity of mcglm has it at zero, it is not zero when the variance depends on the mean, and without it the regression columns of \(\mathbf B\mathbf A^{-1}\) do not vanish under the conditions of the reduced form, where they must. The unit contributions of the first stage are centered: the bias correction is one term for the whole sample rather than a sum over units, so the contributions without it sum to minus it at the estimate, and a term common to all units does not enter the variability.

The first stage is a sum over units only when its covariance is block diagonal over them. With an identity within-response structure the units are the rows, or the clusters when cluster is given. With any other structure cluster is required and has to nest it: every matrix of the matrix linear predictor must vanish between distinct clusters, which is checked.

method = "auto" reads the route from what the fit shows. It takes the full form when the full form is available and at least one response has a variance function other than "constant". With a variance that depends on the mean the shortcut needs condition (c) of the section "What the correction reaches", at least in its weaker form, and that is a statement about the data that cannot be read off the fit. It also takes the full form, when it is available, on a fitted DAG with an immorality: the shortcut evaluates the reduced form at the fitted covariance, which is exact for the parameters of every node of a DAG without immoralities but, for the parameters of a collider with non-adjacent parents and of its descendants, only a first-order approximation under correct specification. In every other case "auto" takes the shortcut when it applies and the full form when it does not. The shortcut, when it applies, is therefore the route in two cases: every response has the constant variance function and the layer is a GGM or a DAG without immoralities, or the full form is not available. On a DAG with an immorality the second case raises a warning. The variance function is read by its name in the first-stage fit, one per response, whatever its power: a Tweedie variance with power fixed at zero counts as depending on the mean, and so does a fit whose names cannot be read. method = "shortcut" and method = "full" force a route, and an explicit "shortcut" is honored without a warning. On the fits both routes cover they agree to first order when the conditions of the section "When the shortcut is right" hold. The attribute "two_stage_method" of the result records the route taken, and mc_two_stage_available reports it beforehand; a fit neither route covers raises an error rather than returning the uncorrected matrix under the corrected name.

What the correction reaches

How much of the propagation reaches a given quantity is settled, for the undirected layer, by a diagonal-rescaling argument, under three conditions on the first stage, which are sufficient and, as the section "When the shortcut is right" says, not always necessary:

(a)

the Pearson residual has the form \(r_{ri}=(y_{ri}-\mu_{ri})/\varsigma_{ri}\), with the mean and the scale depending only on the first-stage parameters and the covariates, which is what mcglm returns;

(b)

the mean is correctly specified, \(E(r_{ri}\mid\mathbf x_i)=0\);

(c)

the conditional residual covariance does not depend on the covariates, \(E(\mathbf r_i\mathbf r_i^\top\mid\mathbf x_i)= \boldsymbol\Sigma_b\).

Under the three, the propagation term is the coordinate vector of \(\mathbf K_b\boldsymbol\Lambda_i+\boldsymbol\Lambda_i\mathbf K_b\), with \(\boldsymbol\Lambda_i\) diagonal: the first stage acts on the residual covariance, to first order, as a diagonal rescaling. The propagation vanishes on every edge whose precision entry is zero and is annihilated by the gradient of every partial correlation, so for those quantities the sandwich and the corrected form agree to first order. The diagonal coefficients and the fitted \(\boldsymbol\Sigma_b\) are not invariant and do need the correction. The DAG layer has the same reading, for any fixed DAG, with the second moment of the residuals in the place of \(\boldsymbol\Sigma_b\) in (c): the propagation vanishes on every structural coefficient whose target value is zero and on every function of the parameters that is invariant to a diagonal rescaling of the residuals, such as the partial correlations, while the nonzero structural coefficients and the innovation variances need the correction.

For the shortcut the agreement on the partial correlations is exact and holds whatever the data: the gradients of the partial correlations annihilate \(\mathbf H^{-1}\mathbf Q\) algebraically, since \(2\mathbf H^{-1}\mathbf Q_{\cdot r}\) is the direction of a rescaling, so type = "sandwich" and the shortcut give them the same variance. That says nothing about whether the variance is right. When the first stage does not act as a rescaling, as can happen with a variance function that depends on the mean and a residual correlation that moves with the covariates, both can miss the same first-order term on the partial correlations, and only the full form accounts for it.

The model-based form \(\mathbf J_n^{-1}\) agrees with the empirical forms only when, in addition, \(\mathbf H=\mathbf J\) and \(\mathbf V=\mathbf J\); the latter is the correctly specified Gaussian fourth-moment regime. Outside it the difference is not a matter of the first stage, and (a) to (c) do not remove it. The package checks none of (a) to (c): they are statements about the process that generated the data. Applied to a support chosen by a search over graphs, every form remains descriptive, since the selection is not incorporated.

References

Bonat, W. H. and Jorgensen, B. (2016). Multivariate covariance generalized linear models. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series C 65(5), 649–675. doi:10.1111/rssc.12145

Godambe, V. P. (1960). An optimum property of regular maximum likelihood estimation. Annals of Mathematical Statistics 31(4), 1208–1211. doi:10.1214/aoms/1177705693

Jorgensen, B. and Knudsen, S. J. (2004). Parameter orthogonality and bias adjustment for estimating functions. Scandinavian Journal of Statistics 31(1), 93–114. doi:10.1111/j.1467-9469.2004.00375.x

Murphy, K. M. and Topel, R. H. (1985). Estimation and inference in two-step econometric models. Journal of Business and Economic Statistics 3(4), 370–379. doi:10.1080/07350015.1985.10509471

Newey, W. K. and McFadden, D. (1994). Large sample estimation and hypothesis testing. In Engle, R. F. and McFadden, D. L. (eds), Handbook of Econometrics, vol. 4, 2111–2245. Elsevier. doi:10.1016/S1573-4412(05)80005-4

White, H. (1980). A heteroskedasticity-consistent covariance matrix estimator and a direct test for heteroskedasticity. Econometrica 48(4), 817–838. doi:10.2307/1912934

See also

mc_test_independence for the joint Wald test, which consumes this matrix, mc_wald_graph for general linear hypotheses, mc_two_stage_available for the route the correction takes, mc_graph_bootstrap for resampling, and mc_partial_cor_delta for the delta-method inference on the partial correlations.

Other inference on the graph layer: mc_test_adequacy(), mc_test_independence(), mc_two_stage_available(), mc_wald_graph()

Examples

# \donttest{
set.seed(1); n <- 300
K <- diag(3) * 2; K[1, 2] <- K[2, 1] <- -0.7
Y <- matrix(rnorm(n * 3), n) %*% chol(solve(K))
d <- data.frame(y1 = Y[, 1], y2 = Y[, 2], y3 = Y[, 3], x = rnorm(n))
f <- mcglm_graph(list(y1 ~ x, y2 ~ x, y3 ~ x), data = d)
#> Automatic initial values selected.
V <- mc_vcov_graph(f, type = "sandwich")
sqrt(diag(V))[attr(V, "edge_pos")]      # standard errors of the edges
#>     eta_12     eta_13     eta_23 
#> 0.07693955 0.06668838 0.05918675 
# }
